title: The Best Time of Year to Seal Concrete in Ontario
metaTitle: Best Time of Year to Seal Concrete in Ontario
metaDescription: Concrete sealing depends on temperature and dry weather, not the calendar month. Here is how to time a driveway or patio sealing project in Southwestern Ontario
excerpt: Sealing concrete is a weather-driven job, not a date on the calendar. Here is how the spring-through-fall window actually works and how to plan around it in Southwestern Ontario.
heroAlt: A concrete patio being sealed on a mild autumn day in Southwestern Ontario with sealer being applied by roller
keyTakeaways: Concrete sealer needs dry surfaces and temperatures roughly between 10 and 30 degrees Celsius, which puts the practical window at spring through fall in Southwestern Ontario.
Spring sealing protects concrete before the heaviest UV, salt and hot-tire exposure of summer, but the surface must be fully dry from snowmelt first.
Fall is a popular window because it seals the surface before winter's freeze-thaw cycles and road salt, which is when concrete is most vulnerable.
Sealing does not happen in freezing temperatures or during wet weather, so booking with some flexibility around the forecast avoids delays.
Most driveways and patios need resealing every 2 to 4 years, so the right time is also a function of when the last coat was applied, not just the season.

body.text: A common question homeowners in London, Woodstock, Brantford, St. Thomas and across Southwestern Ontario ask is simply when the best time to seal their concrete is. The honest answer is that sealing is driven by weather conditions more than by a fixed calendar date. Solvent-based acrylic sealer needs dry concrete and moderate temperatures to bond and cure properly, and in this region that combination shows up reliably across a spring-through-fall window, roughly April through October depending on the year. Understanding how that window works, and how spring and fall compare to each other, makes it easier to plan a sealing project around real conditions rather than guesswork.
Why temperature and moisture set the schedule

Sealer application happens when surfaces are dry and temperatures sit roughly between 10 and 30 degrees Celsius. Below that range, sealer can cure too slowly or unevenly, and cold concrete does not accept the coating the way it does in milder conditions. Above that range, on the hottest summer days, sealer can dry too quickly at the surface before it has fully bonded, which can trap solvent underneath and cause bubbling or an uneven finish. That upper end is less of a concern in this region than the lower end, but it is part of why late spring through early fall, rather than the peak of a July heatwave, tends to be the sweet spot for many projects.

Moisture matters just as much as temperature. Concrete needs to be fully dry, not just dry on the surface, before sealer goes down, which typically means allowing at least 24 to 48 hours after any pressure washing or rainfall before application. That is why a scheduled sealing date sometimes shifts by a day or two around a wet forecast. It is not a scheduling inconvenience so much as a requirement for a sealer that will actually hold up.
The case for sealing in spring

Spring sealing has a clear logic: it protects concrete before the season that puts the most stress on it. Once the snow is gone and the surface has had time to dry out fully from winter meltwater, typically by late April or May in this region, a fresh coat of sealer sets the surface up to handle summer's UV exposure, hot tires in driveways, and pool or patio traffic with a fully cured, protective layer already in place. For anyone whose concrete took a beating over the winter, or who wants a driveway or patio ready to go before summer entertaining season, spring is a natural choice.

The trade-off with spring is that timing depends on how quickly the ground dries out after snowmelt, which varies year to year. A wet spring can push the earliest sealing dates later into May than homeowners might expect, so some flexibility in scheduling helps.
The case for sealing in fall

Fall is, for many homeowners, the more intuitive choice, and it is a strong one. Sealing in September or October puts a fresh protective coat down right before the season that causes the most damage to unsealed or under-protected concrete: winter's freeze-thaw cycles and the road salt that follows. Solvent-based sealer offers strong resistance to salt exposure, which matters significantly once winter road maintenance and driveway de-icing begin. Getting that protection in place before the first freeze is one of the most common reasons TriCity Concrete Sealing sees a busy fall booking season.

Fall conditions in Southwestern Ontario also tend to bring stable, moderate temperatures and lower humidity than mid-summer, which supports even drying and a clean cure. The main constraint is the calendar itself: the window closes once nighttime temperatures start dropping toward freezing, so waiting too long into November risks running out of suitable sealing days before winter sets in.

Neither spring nor fall is objectively better. Spring protects concrete ahead of summer wear, fall protects it ahead of winter's freeze-thaw and salt exposure. The better choice usually comes down to which season is doing the most damage to your specific surface, and when your last sealing was done.
Why summer sealing still happens

Summer falls within the workable temperature range for sealing, and plenty of projects, including new patios, freshly poured driveways and properties preparing for a summer event, get sealed during July and August. The main consideration in summer is scheduling around the hottest, most humid stretches, since very high heat can affect how evenly the sealer dries at the surface. In practice this usually just means avoiding application during a heat warning rather than avoiding summer altogether.
How reseal timing fits into the picture

Most sealed concrete needs a fresh coat every 2 to 4 years, depending on traffic, sun exposure and how much winter salt the surface sees. That interval matters as much as the season when deciding on timing. A driveway sealed three falls ago that is starting to show wear from UV and salt exposure is a good candidate for a fall recoat this year, before another winter puts additional stress on a thinning coating. A patio sealed two summers ago with lighter use might comfortably wait until next spring. Because TriCity Concrete Sealing uses solvent-based sealer, recoats bond seamlessly with the existing coating, re-emulsifying the old layer rather than requiring it to be stripped first, which keeps the reseal process straightforward whenever the timing is right.
What this means for planning a project

For homeowners deciding when to book, the practical takeaway is to plan around the season that matters most for the specific surface, and to build in some flexibility for weather. A driveway that gets heavy winter salt exposure benefits most from fall sealing. A patio that sees intense summer sun and pool traffic might be a better spring candidate. New concrete or a first-time sealing project can generally go ahead any time within the spring-through-fall window, once the concrete has had enough time to cure. Details specific to driveways are covered on /services/driveway-sealing, and patio-specific considerations are on /services/patio-sealing.
Booking around the seasonal window

Because sealing depends on stretches of dry, moderate weather rather than a single ideal date, booking with some lead time gives more flexibility to work around the forecast. This is especially true in fall, when the workable window is shorter and demand tends to be higher as homeowners look to protect their concrete before winter. A free site assessment is the best starting point regardless of season, since it allows TriCity Concrete Sealing to evaluate the surface's current condition, confirm how much drying time is likely needed, and recommend realistic timing based on the forecast.
How Southwestern Ontario's regional climate factors in

London, Woodstock, Brantford, St. Thomas, Stratford, Ingersoll, Tillsonburg, St. Marys, Aylmer and Simcoe share a fairly consistent regional climate, but there are still small differences worth factoring in. Areas closer to Lake Erie and Lake Huron, such as St. Thomas and parts of the Simcoe area, can see slightly more humidity and lake-effect cloud cover than inland communities like Stratford or St. Marys, which can extend drying times marginally during a damp stretch. None of this changes the overall spring-through-fall window, but it is part of why a site assessment considers the specific property rather than applying a single blanket schedule across the whole service area.
New construction and freshly poured concrete

New concrete follows a different timing logic than an existing surface being resealed. Freshly poured concrete needs time to cure before it can be sealed at all, generally a minimum of several weeks depending on the mix and weather conditions, since sealing too early can trap moisture that has not yet fully left the slab during the concrete's initial curing process. For homeowners with a driveway or patio poured in spring, that often means the surface is ready for its first seal sometime in early to mid-summer. A fall pour may not be ready for sealing until the following spring, once curing is complete and the weather window has reopened. This is a common point of confusion, since new concrete's timeline is governed by the curing process itself rather than by the general spring-through-fall sealing season alone.
Getting started

Whether the plan is a spring refresh ahead of summer or a fall coat before winter sets in, the process starts the same way. faq.q: What temperature does it need to be to seal concrete?
faq.a: Sealer application generally needs temperatures roughly between 10 and 30 degrees Celsius, along with dry surface conditions, which is why the workable season in this region runs spring through fall.

faq.q: Is spring or fall better for sealing a driveway?
faq.a: Both work well. Fall sealing protects the surface ahead of winter's freeze-thaw cycles and road salt, which is when concrete is most vulnerable. Spring sealing protects it ahead of summer's UV exposure and hot tires. The better choice depends on your surface's exposure and when it was last sealed.

faq.q: Can concrete be sealed in the summer heat?
faq.a: Yes, summer generally falls within the workable temperature range, though very hot or humid days may need to be avoided since heat can cause the sealer to dry unevenly at the surface.

faq.q: How soon after it rains can concrete be sealed?
faq.a: Concrete needs to be fully dry before sealing, which usually means allowing at least 24 to 48 hours after rain or pressure washing, depending on humidity and sun exposure.

faq.q: How often does concrete need to be resealed?
faq.a: Most driveways, patios and walkways need resealing every 2 to 4 years, depending on traffic, sun exposure and winter salt use. A free site assessment can confirm whether your surface is due.

faq.q: Can I book a sealing appointment without knowing the exact date the weather will cooperate?
faq.a: Yes. TriCity Concrete Sealing works within a general seasonal window and adjusts the exact appointment date around the forecast to make sure conditions are right for a proper cure.
